column3: Confirms fire-punishment for disbelievers as an outcome; it adds no preventive dimension.
Establishes God-conscious restraint as a fundamental orientation sustained until death.
States that Hell is shown to disbelievers; it does not develop preparation or restraint.
Makes restraint a shared practice alongside patience, mutual steadfastness, and committed watchfulness.
Uses the same formula of a fire prepared for disbelievers; its fuel of people and stones makes the threat concrete.
Links the absence of any protector and the greater final punishment to the need for protection formed beforehand.
Draws attention to fire without developing the relation of restraint or preparation.
Extends restraint into a protective measure spanning what lies before and behind, oriented toward mercy.
Stresses confrontation with the fire they denied, supporting the warning function of 3:131.
The strong parallel makes restraint a boundary against harm in private speech; the rejected contrary route remains preserved.
States a painful punishment prepared for disbelievers, but lacks the fire-and-restraint connection.
A rejected contrary route promotes cooperation in goodness and restraint; it is not direct support for 3:131.
Says no one can repel punishment from disbelievers; it does not develop the protective orientation.
Shows that bringing and affirming truth characterizes the God-conscious, adding the substantive content of restraint.
Places a prepared garden for the God-conscious as the opposite outcome, completing 3:131's fire warning.
Joins seeking forgiveness with seeking protection from fire-punishment, adding dependence on divine protection.
Makes restraint a social boundary that prevents public humiliation.
Makes worship the ground of restraint, without the detail of fire or preparation.
Connects restraint to the Creator and earlier generations, providing a general foundation.
Presents restraint and obedience as a corrective that breaks a coercive social chain.
Relates restraint to awareness of the provisions given, complementing 26:131.
Presents the Book as guidance for the God-conscious; it remains indirect to 3:131's threatened outcome.
Unites the protected outcome of the God-conscious and the fire-outcome of disbelievers in one contrast.
Makes selective, limit-aware obedience a concrete form of restraint; it closely parallels 26:131.
Links a prepared garden to believers; it is a less direct positive counterpart than 3:133.
Balances present and future good with the request for protection from fire-punishment.
Connects following the revealed Book, restraint, and mercy; its fire relation is indirect.
Translates restraint into market conduct through full measure, right weighing, and non-deprivation.
Sustains restraint amid ritual days and awareness of gathering, without explaining the fire outcome.
Shows measured retribution as a life-preserving limit on escalating violence.
Contrasts the garden of the God-conscious with remaining in fire; it parallels 13:35 in greater detail.
Questions the lack of restraint that should discipline power, rather than any lack of power itself.
States the outcome of entering the greatest fire, adding no new protective dimension.
Frames a brotherly warning from within the community as a call to restraint.
Points to the Hell denied by offenders, without establishing a restraint relation.
Shows restraint opening onto a livable protective setting of shade and springs.
States a blazing punishment prepared for disbelievers, supporting 3:131's fiery outcome.
Stresses that verbally recognizing sovereignty must become restraint in conduct.
States arrival in Hell as an outcome, adding no call to prior protection.
Shows denial in the face of recognized confirming knowledge as a value-diminishing exchange.
States a humiliating punishment prepared for disbelievers; the protective dimension is indirect.
Re-establishes the theme of a protective warning from within the community in Noah's setting.
Extends the enduring Hell outcome to hypocrites and disbelievers, without a restraint command.
Directly makes protecting oneself and one's family from the fire a responsibility.
States that return may bring mercy while repeated return brings a Hell outcome.
Explains protection from evils as mercy's active barrier and as the great success.
Reports respite for denial and eventual seizure, only indirectly related to 3:131.
Makes fasting training in consciously placing oneself behind a limit.
States that Hell is prepared for disbelievers, without the accompanying call to protection.
States success for the God-conscious, briefly supporting the opposite outcome of 3:131.
States the fire-punishment they denied, without explaining how restraint operates.
Expands God-consciousness into an integrated practice of faith, giving, covenant, and endurance.
States prepared punishment in the context of wrongful gain; its added link to 3:131 is limited.
Shows the absence of restraint as the inner cause of repeated covenant-breaking.
States divine opposition to disbelievers, without fire or restraint explanation.
Presents the reminder as a signpost leading the God-conscious to a good return.
Warns against supporting disbelievers; it is indirect to 3:131's fire-protection relation.
Asks how protection can be possible with denial, showing that disbelief does not provide real protection.
Makes fire enclosing from above and below the rationale for the preventive call to restraint.
Makes restraint concrete as refusing earthly elevation and corruption.
States prepared punishment in a context of stinginess and concealment; it adds little to the focus verse.
Establishes communal unity under one Lord as restraint's shared orientation.
Describes opportunistic alliances and final judgment; the fire-protection relation is not explicit.
Shows divine protection preventing intended harm from reaching the believer and enclosing its planners instead.
Clarifies the link between denying truth and the Hell outcome of disbelievers.
Contrasts the mutual alliance of wrongdoers with God's guardianship of the God-conscious as protective nearness.
Displays the claim that fire will last only a limited time as false security, clarifying 3:131's immediate context.
Shows that even powerful earlier communities had no protector against God.
States severe punishment for disbelievers, offering general support without a restraint command.
Shows the Lord giving what benefits while keeping Hell-punishment outside, as two-sided protection.
Describes the direction of disbelief through the light-darkness contrast; it is indirect to the focus verse.
Carries restraint into responsibility for protecting shared origin and kinship bonds.
Confirms the Hell outcome of inventing lies about God and denying truth.
Presents protection as active divine intervention that stops an inward-penetrating scorching punishment.
Only addresses disbelievers; it adds no explanatory link to 3:131.
Establishes an outcome distinction between the God-conscious and the corrupt or sinful.
Questions the claim that fire lasts only numbered days as false security; it closely parallels 3:24.
Joins worship and restraint as orientation toward the real protecting authority.
Makes restraint a barrier formed in advance by an intellect that grasps the link between reckoning and outcome.
Holds forgiveness and protection from approaching Hell-punishment as two distinct layers of defense.
The light-darkness contrast alone adds no clear explanation of 3:131.
Makes the call to worship God alone a protective correction of direction; it closely parallels 23:32.
Makes restraint concrete through limits in separation and an order that prevents injustice.
Shows the prophet's presence within the community as making the protective call accessible.
Makes vigilance and arms an example of concrete protection, then adds prepared punishment for disbelievers.
Presents the most God-conscious person's removal from fire as the union of inward and outward protection.
Relates the guardians and number of the fire to testing; it offers limited contribution to 3:131.
Joins restraint and doing good as the two-part attitude to which divine presence is attached.
States that denial will be followed by knowing, without detail of fire or restraint.
Shows believers who practiced restraint being separated and rescued from destruction.
States a brief respite for disbelievers, adding no explanation of 3:131's protective logic.
Sets immorality and God-consciousness as opposing directions: one breaches limits and the other stops harm.
Explains the outcome of being returned to fire whenever escape is attempted, without a restraint dimension.
Shows reward for faith and restraint as concerning human orientation rather than an exploitative demand.
Links choosing punishment over guidance and forgiveness to the fire outcome.
Makes commanding restraint a concrete act of forming a barrier against harmful obedience.
States the fire outcome of a mutually exploitative partnership, without explaining restraint.
Presents restraint as a protective passage integrated with mercy, guiding light, and forgiveness.
States that guidance is a divine responsibility, without opening 3:131's fire-and-restraint link.
Presents restraint as a protective order with the covering of evils and a great reward.
The immediately preceding ban on financial excess supplies the close behavioral context for 3:131's call to restraint.
The immediately following call to obedience and mercy completes the positive end toward which restraint from fire is directed.
Defines success as being drawn away from fire and admitted to the garden, directly explaining 3:131's protective outcome.
